Overview

Salvaging cells and signal in multiplexed single-cell experiments: overview

83 records cited in the text

In this chapter

  1. By stage
  2. What cuts across the stages
  3. The evidence gaps
  4. Chapters

Highly multiplexed single-cell experiments, drug screens above all, spend their cells thinly: hundreds of conditions, tens to a few hundred cells each, often one well per condition. Every step between the plate and the count matrix loses cells, and in published comparisons the losses are large: fixed QC cut-offs alone kept a median 69.4% of cells where cluster-aware thresholds kept up to 95.4% (self-reported, ddqc), weak hashing left 7 to 33% of cells untagged (mylka-2022-hashing-comparison), and only 16.5 to 53% of input cells reached the final data across platforms (split-pool-input-recovery). The losses are also not random. Hashing fails more often in dying and some cell types (mylka-2022-hashing-comparison, hadge), mitochondrial filters remove viable and even drug-resistant malignant cells (mito-filter-resistant-cells), and drugs change how much RNA a cell holds (PMID 34159316). In a screen, a loss that differs by condition is a bias before it is a cost.

This overview summarises five literature reviews written for this hub in October 2026 (129 records and 38 benchmark studies, every identifier fetched and checked). It is organised by pipeline stage: what is standard, what has won an independent benchmark, what is published but untested, and what is only proposed. The short version:

  1. Recover tagged cells with a better caller, not a looser one. Per-cell normalisation of tag counts and RNA-aware or free-tag-aware callers recover most cells wrongly called negative (sayed-2025-hashtag-benchmark, demuxmix, deMULTIplex2); genotypes rescue most of the rest when samples differ genetically (hadge).
  2. Keep cells by replacing single-metric cut-offs with evidence that separates damage from biology: test barcodes against the ambient profile (EmptyDrops), compute thresholds within cell type and batch (ddqc, miQC), use the nuclear fraction for damage (DropletQC), and correct ambient RNA instead of discarding mixed profiles (CellBender remove-background, DecontX).
  3. Borrow strength, do not invent replicates. Pseudobulk with the culture or well as the unit leads every independent benchmark (squair-2021, junttila-2022); weighting small samples (dreamlet), empirical Bayes (Empirical Bayes moderation), dose as a trend (Dose-response modelling across doses) and multivariate shrinkage across conditions (mashr) add power without pretending cells are replicates (cell-subsample-pseudoreplicates).
  4. Design for replicates and for fixing early. Duplicate wells with randomised positions (sci-Plex, Independent replicate wells or cultures per condition), fixation at harvest (10x Chromium Flex, Methanol fixation) and tagged superloading (Superloading with sample multiplexing, modelled rather than benchmarked) change usable cells and true replicates more than any downstream tool.
  5. Treat what is discarded as data. Cells lost per condition track toxicity (Cell recovery per condition as a viability readout), survivors can hide a drug's effect (survivor-bias), and doublets can be real cell contacts (PIC-seq, Neighbor-seq). None of these has been tested as a readout in a high-multiplex drug screen.

Tiers follow the hub schema. "Benchmarked best" means best or tied best in at least one study by other authors (38 benchmark studies are listed in the catalog); "mixed" means independently evaluated without being best, or with conflicting results. Several wins rest on one benchmark, and some conflict: demuxmix led one hashing benchmark but failed on imbalanced xenograft pools in another.

What cuts across the stages

Losses depend on the condition. Every stage loses more cells from stressed, damaged or atypical cells: weak tags in dying cells (mylka-2022-hashing-comparison), low-RNA treated cells at cell calling, high-mito resistant cells at QC (mito-filter-resistant-cells). In a drug screen this means a QC step can remove part of a drug's effect, or create one. The cheapest protection is an audit: cells kept per condition at each step, tested for dependence on the condition (condition-aware-qc-audit).

Hashing is an independent witness. Tags measure that a cell was present independently of its RNA, so they help decide whether a QC-flagged cell is damaged or merely different, and they can rescue cells below RNA thresholds (MULTI-seq, Tag-guided rescue of low-RNA cells).

More cells per condition is not more replicates. Splitting one well's cells into groups reproduces the bias and false discoveries of cell-level tests (cell-subsample-pseudoreplicates, squair-2021). With one culture per condition, a p-value says that two wells differ, not that a drug works. The large screens differ sharply here: sci-Plex used duplicate wells, Tahoe-100M one well per drug and dose.

Models are not a substitute for replicates. Deep perturbation models have not beaten additive or linear baselines in independent comparisons (ahlmann-eltze-2025), and imputation mostly erases small effects (imputation-de-evidence).

The evidence gaps

  • No step of the salvage pipeline has been benchmarked on drug-treated cells.
  • No independent benchmark of cell callers or of adaptive QC tools exists.
  • No hashing benchmark goes beyond about 24 tags or tests row-by-column (combinatorial) tag designs.
  • No study compares minimum-cell cut-offs with weighting by cell number, or tests signals in discarded barcodes as readouts in drug screens.

These gaps are where a well-designed screen could contribute evidence of its own.

Chapter 01

Recovering cells at demultiplexing

25 records reviewed here, 35 records cited in the text

In this chapter

  1. Standard practice
  2. Benchmarked state of the art
  3. Published but not independently benchmarked
  4. Hypotheses and open questions
  5. Practical recommendations for low-cell multiplexed drug screens
  6. Records in this chapter

Demultiplexing is the first place a multiplexed experiment loses cells, and the losses are larger and less random than they look. On well-hashed pools the main callers agree and lose little: in the cleanest batch of an independent benchmark every hashtag caller scored a mean F of 0.88 to 0.94 against genotype truth (Howitt 2023, howitt-2023-hto-benchmark), and antibody-hashed cell lines left only 1.1 to 1.8% of cells as tagless negatives (Mylka 2022, mylka-2022-hashing-comparison). On weak hashing the picture changes. Lipid tags left 7 to 21% of cells negative on the same cell lines, antibody tags left 33% of nuclei negative, and on a poorly hashed tumour batch the callers' mean F ranged from 0 to 0.68 while genotypes still placed 90% of droplets as singlets (Howitt 2023). Three levers recover most of what is lost. First, the caller and its normalisation: per-cell instead of per-tag normalisation recovered about 56 to 97% of the cells wrongly called negative for the tag with the most variable depth in one benchmark (Sayed 2025, sayed-2025-hashtag-benchmark). Second, genotypes, when samples differ genetically: a hashing plus genotype rescue recovered 89.7% of hashing negatives in hashed brain nuclei (Curion 2024, hadge). Third, not discarding single cells that hashing mislabels as doublets, a problem that grows with the number of tags (Li 2024, HTOreader and hybrid hashing-genotype demultiplexing). For a drug screen in which every condition is applied to the same cell line, only the first and third levers apply, because genotype can tell cell lines apart but not drugs.

Standard practice

The default workflow runs one caller with default settings and keeps its singlets. In Seurat that is HTODemux: tag counts are centred-log-ratio (CLR) normalised per tag, droplets are clustered, a negative binomial is fitted to each tag's background cluster, and a droplet is positive for a tag above the 0.99 quantile of that background (Stoeckius 2018). The Seurat vignette runs exactly these defaults; on its 8-tag example they give 13 972 singlets, 2 598 doublets and 346 negatives. MULTIseqDemux / deMULTIplex (the MULTI-seq classifier, McGinnis 2019) is the other Seurat option. In Python, scanpy ships HashSolo; in Bioconductor, DropletUtils provides hashedDrops.

When samples come from different people or different cell lines, genotype demultiplexing is the standard alternative or complement. demuxlet / freemuxlet needs reference genotypes; in its original simulation 50 SNPs per cell assigned 97% of singlets in pools of up to 64 people (Kang 2018). vireo and souporcell need no reference and infer genotypes from the pooled reads (Huang 2019; Heaton 2020). For pooled cancer cell lines, the MIX-Seq design classifies cells with as few as 50 to 100 detected SNP sites and agreed with expression-based calls for over 99% of cells (McFarland 2020, see MIX-Seq).

Standard practice discards negatives and all hashing doublets. Two facts make that costly. Hashing quality and RNA quality were "largely uncorrelated" across the Howitt datasets, so a weak tag does not mean a bad cell. And the cells that fail to tag are not a random sample: antibody-hashed mouse brain left mostly non-microglial cells negative, dying high-mitochondrial PBMC clusters hashed worse (Mylka 2022), and two neuronal clusters among hashed brain nuclei consisted mostly or entirely of cells that hashing had dropped (Curion 2024).

Benchmarked state of the art

Hashing callers. Howitt 2023 compared seven callers against vireo genotype assignments on six tagging experiments with antibody and lipid tags. Genotypes called 81 to 91% of droplets singlets, more than any hashtag caller except BFFcluster, which over-called singlets. demuxmix was best overall, scoring mean F 0.907, 0.833 and 0.775 on three bronchoalveolar lavage batches and calling under 20% of genetic doublets singlets; HTODemux and GMM-Demux were close. Callers that assume two clean peaks per tag collapsed on weak data: BFFcluster (cellhashR) fell to 0.119 and 0.188 on the weaker lavage batches and deMULTIplex to 0.218 on a tumour batch. HashSolo left the fewest negatives of any caller except BFFcluster but called about 30% (lavage) to 60% (cell lines) of genetic doublets singlets. Lowering hashedDrops's threshold gave the best F in four of six batches, at the price of roughly doubling doublet leakage, about 3 000 extra doublets in one batch. The authors' advice for weak hashing is to try several callers to maximise singlets, while watching doublets.

Mylka 2022 compared tag chemistries and preferred MULTIseqDemux / deMULTIplex: overall classification accuracy 0.96 for antibody-hashed cell lines, against 0.68 to 0.84 for lipid tags; for nuclei, cholesterol-oligo tags reached 0.84 (0.74 with HTODemux) and antibody tags 0.51 to 0.54. Changing HTODemux's positive quantile from 0.99 to 0.9 raised the antibody-nuclei accuracy from 0.54 to 0.65, a direct measure of how much the default cut-off leaves behind. Antibodies were better for spleen and lung, lipids for brain (0.85 to 0.87 against 0.38). On hashed brain nuclei, MULTI-seq and demuxEM, which models each tag's background from empty droplets, matched vireo's donors best of the hashing tools, while HashSolo called almost every droplet a singlet and hashedDrops called 32 singlets out of 4 048 droplets (Curion 2024). Caller choice alone can swing yield from almost nothing to almost everything on nuclei.

Sayed 2025 crossed normalisations with callers on 12 real datasets. Normalising tags within each cell, so that a cell's shallow tag library does not push it under every threshold, separated tagged from untagged cells better than the per-tag CLR in the Seurat vignette. On the dataset with the most variable tag depth it recovered about 97% (clustering) and 56% (MULTI-seq workflow) of the cells wrongly called negative for one tag. A per-cell CLR plus clustering workflow (hashDemux) had the highest average F; its doublet calls were weak, so RNA-based doublet filtering should follow.

deMULTIplex2 models how free tags contaminate droplets. Its own benchmark reports 63.2% of all cells correctly assigned on a multiplexed breast-cancer xenograft dataset against 50.8% for its predecessor, two samples recovered that other callers missed, over 99% recall in a 30-sample imbalanced simulation where HTODemux reached 52% and demuxmix (without RNA) 73%, and stable accuracy at about 10 cells per sample (Zhu 2024). In outside comparisons it was near the top: F 0.87 against 0.9 for the best workflow in Sayed 2025, and 79% concordance with vireo on the poorly hashed tumours against 81% for CMDdemux, both ahead of other callers (Wang 2026, CMDdemux). The same CMDdemux comparison found deMULTIplex2 and BFF failing on an over-labelled CellPlex xenograft dataset. No single caller wins everywhere.

Genotype callers. On simulated single-nucleus pools, vireo was the most accurate and fastest of vireo, souporcell, freemuxlet and scSplit; all but scSplit reached 80 to 85% accuracy (Fu 2025, fu-2025-snrna-genetic-benchmark). In pooled tumours with heavy copy-number change, vireo with bulk RNA-seq genotypes recalled 99.0 to 99.9% of singlets, and 99.2% of its doublet calls were real against 31.9% for demuxlet (Weber 2021, weber-2021-cancer-genetic-demux). Demuxafy compared seven genotype tools on 74 PBMC pools and 70 simulated pools of 2 to 128 donors: Demuxalot had the fewest errors (about 1% at 2 donors, 3% at 16 or more), vireo was the best single tool without reference genotypes at 16 or more donors, souporcell and vireo were unaffected by added ambient RNA up to 16 donors, and souporcell degraded above 32 (Neavin 2024). Combining tools raised Matthews correlation by about 0.09. Precision falls as doublets rise for every genotype tool (Fu 2025): vireo's went from 100% to 77.4% between 0% and 30% simulated doublets (Weber 2021).

Published but not independently benchmarked

Hybrid rescue. When samples are genetically distinct, genotype clusters can be named by the hashtag that dominates them, and every cell in a cluster then gets a sample label whatever its tag looked like. hadge runs 7 hashing and 5 genotype tools in one Nextflow pipeline; its rescue mode called 90% of hashed brain nuclei singlets, rescued 89.7% of hashing negatives, doubled singlets for the weakest tags, and after the original study's QC kept 3 208 cells, 952 of which had been excluded before (Curion 2024). HTOreader and hybrid hashing-genotype demultiplexing added 5.2% singlets to an 8-donor pool, most of them cells hashing had called doublets (715) or negatives (166), and assigned 88% of cells across a hashed pool and an unhashed pool from the same donors; about 100 hashtagged cells per donor were enough to name the clusters (Li 2024). demuxSNP trains a nearest-neighbour classifier on confident hashing singlets' SNP profiles and reassigns negatives, uncertain cells and doublets; on renal cancer data HTODemux had left over 10% of cells negative (Lynch 2024). All three need genetic differences between samples; souporcell, the clustering step in HTOreader, produced wrong clusters at high doublet rates in two of these papers.

Using the tag to keep low-RNA cells. MULTI-seq showed that a confident tag is evidence a barcode holds a cell even when its RNA is too low for standard cell calling: 90.8% of sequenced neutrophils in cryopreserved xenografts fell below the Cell Ranger UMI inflection and were kept because their barcodes classified, while unclassified low-RNA barcodes looked like broken cells (McGinnis 2019, Tag-guided rescue of low-RNA cells). The cell-calling side of this is covered under EmptyDrops and CellBender remove-background.

Newer callers. CMDdemux normalises tags within each cell, clusters, classifies by Mahalanobis distance with mRNA information and reports gains on low-quality and over-labelled data (Wang 2026). GMM-Demux also estimates how many same-sample doublets remain undetectable, and flagged 9 multiplet-made clusters in PBMC (Xin 2020). Several 2023 to 2026 tools were noted but not given records: scDemultiplex (beta-binomial, PMID 37664174), Ensemblex (genotype ensemble for 4 to 80 lines; 90.12% of cells correctly classified, PMID 40611203), Souporcell3 (up to 64 donors, PMID 41808435), mitoSplitter (mitochondrial variants, used on five lung cancer lines under a BET degrader, PMID 37725654), fastdemux (preprint, PMID 41726916) and CellBouncer CellBouncer.

Hypotheses and open questions

Doublets. A true cross-condition doublet cannot be rescued; its RNA is a mixture of two conditions. Studies that use hashing doublets as ground truth found 73% of hashing multiplets were missed by every RNA-based detector (Ttoouli 2025, PMID 41166377).

Assigning untagged cells from their transcriptome. For fixed identities this works: cell-line calls from expression and from SNPs agreed for over 99% of MIX-Seq cells, and expression-aware demultiplexing of donors reached mean accuracy 0.98 when combined with genetics (Nassiri 2024, PMID 38911824). For treatment labels it is circular: a cell assigned to a drug because it looks treated will inflate that drug's effect and hide non-responders (expression-label-recovery).

Gaps. No benchmark has tested callers at more than about 24 tags per pool, on drug-treated cells, or on row-by-column tag designs. In a two-group design a well is known only when both the row call and the column call are singlets, so well-level yield is roughly the product of the two singlet rates; this follows from the design and has not been measured (designs are covered under sci-Plex, MULTI-seq and SPLiT-seq / Parse Evercode). The consensus mode of cellhashR and the intersections in Demuxafy have not been compared with single callers on hashing data. No evidence was found that the tag-counting tool (Cell Ranger, CITE-seq-Count, kallisto) changes recovery.

Practical recommendations for low-cell multiplexed drug screens

Ranked by expected gain per unit of effort, for screens with many conditions and few cells per condition.

  1. Diagnose before choosing. Plot each tag's count distribution and a tag-space embedding, then tabulate negatives, doublets and median tag UMIs per condition (Howitt 2023 gives the plots). Gain: none by itself, but it shows whether losses are small and even (then stop) or large and condition-specific. Needs: tag counts.
  2. Re-call with per-cell normalisation and more than one caller. Run HTODemux on per-cell CLR (Seurat margin 2), demuxmix with the RNA covariate, and deMULTIplex2; keep cells that agree, inspect cells on which they disagree. Do not tune thresholds just to raise singlet counts (hashedDrops doubled doublet leakage that way). Expected gain: little on clean data (all callers within about 0.06 F of each other in Howitt 2023), tens of percent of negatives on weak or imbalanced data (Sayed 2025; Zhu 2024, self-reported). Needs: tag counts, RNA counts.
  3. Add genotypes if the pool holds more than one cell line or donor. Run vireo or souporcell (or Demuxalot with reference genotypes) and rescue with hadge, HTOreader and hybrid hashing-genotype demultiplexing or demuxSNP. Expected gain: 70 to 90% of hashing negatives in the one dataset measured (Curion 2024) plus misfiled doublets. Genotype recovers the cell line, not the drug: a rescued cell gets a condition only if each line received one condition in that pool. Needs: BAM, genetically distinct samples.
  4. Look at low-RNA tagged barcodes before RNA QC. Treated cells may shrink or lose RNA; keep confidently tagged low-RNA barcodes for review instead of cutting them at a UMI floor (Tag-guided rescue of low-RNA cells). Gain: cell-type dependent. Needs: raw matrix and tags.
  5. Use expression-based assignment only for identity. Recover cell line or cell type for negatives if needed, never the drug (expression-label-recovery).
  6. Design the next run for recovery. Antibody tags for intact cells and lipid or cholesterol tags for nuclei and brain (Mylka 2022); titrate and process quickly (Brown 2024, PMID 38220132); balance loading across conditions; sequence tags enough, since deMULTIplex2 kept near-perfect accuracy at a median of 30 tag counts per cell on clean data. Where hashing is the bottleneck, genotype-pooled cell lines (MIX-Seq) or well-barcoded chemistries (sci-Plex, 10x Chromium Flex, SPLiT-seq / Parse Evercode) avoid tag loss altogether. Statistical handling of the few cells left per condition is covered under dreamlet and muscat.

Chapter 02

Keeping cells at cell calling and QC; damaged cells

23 records reviewed here, 48 records cited in the text

In this chapter

  1. How many cells are thrown away that could be kept, and how to keep them safely
  2. Standard practice
  3. Benchmarked state of the art
  4. Published but not independently benchmarked
  5. Damage or biology: how to tell
  6. Hypotheses and open questions
  7. Recommendations for low-cell multiplexed drug screens
  8. Records in this chapter

Scope: separating cells from empty droplets, ambient RNA removal as a way to keep cells, QC thresholds, damaged and dying cells, and RNA-based doublet detection where it changes what is kept. Tag-based demultiplexing and tag doublets are covered in the demultiplexing review (demuxmix, HTODemux); statistics with few cells per condition in the low-cell review (Pseudobulk differential expression).

How many cells are thrown away that could be kept, and how to keep them safely

Two steps decide which barcodes become cells: cell calling, then QC filtering. Both discard intact cells, and the published numbers are large.

Cell calling. A total-UMI threshold cannot tell a small cell from an empty droplet, so knee-style calling loses low-RNA cell types. EmptyDrops kept a putative interneuron cluster in a ~900-cell brain dataset and putative monocytes in placenta that the Cell Ranger v2 knee discarded EmptyDrops. Callers built on it report more: CB2 found 24% more cells than EmptyDrops on average (range 4-81%), 88% of them joining existing populations CB2, and EmptyNN recovered 885 barcodes below a 200-UMI cut, including platelets with a median of 93.5 UMIs EmptyNN. These gains are self-reported. The opposite error is real too: after EmptyDrops, DropletQC still found 0.4% (PBMC) to 9.5% (mouse brain) of called barcodes to be cell-free DropletQC.

Dying cells are lost before any software sees them. In cells sorted after TNF-alpha treatment, 885 dying and 1,280 dead cells were recovered against 3,000 targeted oflanagan-2019. Drug-treated cells may also carry less RNA: paclitaxel or celecoxib alone generally repressed global transcription per cell when measured against spike-ins (PMID 34159316).

QC filtering. Fixed mitochondrial cut-offs remove the most. A 10% cut removed 41% of cells from a menstrual blood dataset where miQC removed 19%, and 88.1% of one ovarian tumour sample miQC. Across many datasets, a fixed rule (<200 genes or >10% mito) retained a median 69.4% of cells against up to 95.4% for cluster-level adaptive QC ddqc. A 5% mito cut misclassified healthy and low-quality cells in 13 of 44 human tissues osorio-cai-2021, and high-mito malignant cells are viable, with no more dissociation stress than other malignant cells mito-filter-resistant-cells.

Keeping them safely means replacing single-metric cut-offs with evidence that separates damage from biology: testing barcodes against the ambient profile rather than a UMI floor, computing thresholds within cell type and batch, using the nuclear (unspliced) fraction as a damage signal, and correcting ambient RNA rather than discarding cells with mixed profiles. Each is covered below with its evidence.

Standard practice

  • Cell calling. Cell Ranger calls cells in two steps: an order-of-magnitude UMI cut-off for high-RNA cells, then an EmptyDrops-style test for low-RNA cells (10x Genomics documentation; Cell Ranger). STARsolo's default is a Cell Ranger 2.2-style knee; its EmptyDrops_CR option copies Cell Ranger 3/4 and hard-codes Cell Ranger's candidate limits, including a 500-UMI minimum (umiMin) and a minimum fraction of the median cell (umiMinFracMedian 0.01), so lower barcodes are never tested (STAR documentation, docs/STARsolo.md; STARsolo, Knee / inflection-point cell calling). DropletUtils' emptyDrops treats barcodes at or below 100 UMIs as ambient and tests everything above EmptyDrops.
  • QC thresholds. Best-practice guides use thresholds relative to each sample: the scverse guide flags cells 5 median absolute deviations (MADs) from the median on log counts, log genes and top-20-gene share, and mito only when it is both 3 MADs high and above 8%, and advises being "as permissive as possible" (heumos-2023; sc-best-practices.org). Bioconductor's OSCA uses scuttle's MAD outliers per batch osca. See MAD-based adaptive QC thresholds.
  • Ambient RNA. The scverse guide runs SoupX; DecontX and CellBender remove-background are the common alternatives.
  • Doublets. The scverse guide uses scDblFinder; Scrublet and DoubletFinder remain widely used.
  • Bench side. Dead-cell and apoptotic-cell exclusion before loading is recommended but often skipped (PMID 31603610).

Benchmarked state of the art

Ambient RNA. Three independent benchmarks agree that no method wins everywhere.

  • Janssen et al. pooled two mouse subspecies so that cross-genotype reads measure background directly. Background made up 3-35% of UMIs per cell, mostly ambient RNA. CellBender gave the most precise per-cell estimates and the largest gain in marker detection: the proximal tubule marker Slc34a1 appeared in ~60% of non-tubule cells before correction, 54% after SoupX, 7% after CellBender and 2% after DecontX. SoupX underestimated background and, by design, cannot capture cell-to-cell variation. Clustering was fairly robust to noise janssen-2023.
  • Cargnelli et al. tested seven methods on 64 samples (135,561 cells), including control samples without ambient RNA. 81.56% of cells carried some ambient RNA (mean load 7.79% in cells, 11.80% in nuclei). scAR (0.679) and CellBender (0.604) removed the most ambient RNA, but scAR also removed 0.445 of endogenous signal; DecontX was the only method that did not reduce cell-type recovery. They recommend CellBender, DecontX in full mode, or SoupX in reduced mode, noting that CellBender and DecontX over-correct clean samples more than SoupX cargnelli-2026.
  • Nie et al. tested seven tools on ten metrics. The abstract names DecontX most accurate for contamination level, scAR most robust but overestimating, and CellClear best for closely related subtypes. In their mitochondrial-genotype experiment, CellBender and FastCAR came closest to the measured baseline (mean RMSLE below 0.06); scAR reassigned ~17% of cells to other types in one dataset nie-2026.
  • Two 2026 preprints extend this, so the summary below is not final. Schroeder et al. added a well-plate platform and a count-integrity check: CellBender and SoupX removed contamination reliably with minimal distortion, while scAR created spurious cell types and CellClear replaced most counts schroeder-2026. Meier et al. found doublet detection worked best before ambient correction, except with CellBender meier-2026. Both are covered in the quantification and ambient review.

Readers should note the conflict inside Nie et al.: abstract and results name different winners for contamination accuracy. On present evidence, CellBender remove-background and DecontX are benchmarked state of the art, scAR is the most aggressive (good removal, real over-correction risk), and SoupX is the conservative standard.

Doublets. Xi and Li benchmarked nine detectors on 16 real datasets with annotated doublets and 112 synthetic ones; DoubletFinder was most accurate and cxds fastest xi-li-2021. In their protocol extension, scDblFinder had the highest mean AUPRC and AUROC on the same 16 datasets (PMID 34382023), which singletCode replicated singletcode-2024. pipeComp found that doublet calls and MAD-based outliers barely overlap, so a high-UMI cut-off is not a doublet filter pipeComp. The caveat for drug screens is in singletCode: on lineage-barcoded data with ground-truth singlets, mean AUPRC was 0.13-0.34 for all four detectors tested, lowest for scDblFinder singletcode-2024. RNA-based detectors find doublets of different cell types; a screen of one cell line produces mostly same-type doublets, which only tags or genotypes can see.

QC thresholds. The only independent benchmark of filtering stringency is pipeComp. Filtering against the whole population removed subpopulations with extreme but healthy properties such as large library size; clustering accuracy plateaued and then fell as stringency rose; its recommendation is 5 MADs, or 3 MADs on at least two metrics pipeComp. No independent benchmark of the adaptive QC tools below exists.

Cell calling. No independent benchmark of cell callers was found. The closest is the valiDrops paper, which ran seven callers on a 10x 8k PBMC sample: most called ~8,000 barcodes, dropkick and EmptyNN over 9,000 valiDrops.

Published but not independently benchmarked

Cell callers. CB2 (above). dropkick learns a cell-versus-empty model per sample; on high-background simulations its specificity was 0.9999 against 0.9910 for the Cell Ranger v2 knee and 0.9838 for EmptyDrops, and on colorectal inDrop data it recovered more cells from rare populations while removing more dead cells dropkick. SiftCell SiftCell and DIEM for nuclei DIEM target high-ambient data. CellBender also calls cells, but its calls have not been benchmarked separately CellBender remove-background.

Adaptive QC.

  • miQC models mito fraction against genes detected as a mixture of intact and compromised cells. Besides the numbers above: pancreas, 7.8% removed against 45.5% at 10% mito; in six ovarian tumours 8.1-49.0% against 8.6-94.8%, though miQC removed more in one of the six. A fixed cut-off also removed 6.8% or 14.6% of the same library depending on the reference genome; miQC removed 10.6% and 8.8%.
  • ddqc clusters first and applies MAD thresholds within clusters on genes, UMIs, mito and ribosomal fractions, keeping neutrophils and metabolically active parenchymal cells. miQC removed a cardiomyocyte cluster (median 15% mito) that ddqc kept.
  • MitoChontrol (preprint) fits a mixture to mito fraction within each cluster. On HEK293 data with mito RNA inflated in 10% of cells, it removed the inflated subset and kept the rest, while ddqc kept many inflated cells; no removal counts are reported.
  • scQCenrich adds intronic fraction, MALAT1 enrichment and stress features. On 10x mouse brain it removed 1,185 cells against 2,520 (Seurat-style), 1,801 (scater), 2,770 (miQC) and 1,968 (DropletQC).
  • SampleQC fits a multivariate mixture across samples and cell types and was less likely to exclude rare types in simulations SampleQC.

Damage detection. DropletQC uses the nuclear fraction, the share of reads from unspliced pre-mRNA. Damaged cells have lost cytoplasmic RNA, so they show high nuclear fraction and low UMIs; empty droplets show ambient-like, mostly spliced profiles. Among EmptyDrops calls it flagged 5.2-14.0% damaged cells in three tissues and almost none in PBMC; cryopreservation raised the damaged share from 4.1% to 13.8%. DamageDetective (CRAN, 2025) scores cells against simulated copies with cytoplasmic RNA removed; no paper was found.

Ambient, gene-specific and DE-oriented. scCDC corrects only the genes that cause contamination and reports that DecontX and CellBender under-correct those genes while SoupX and scAR over-correct housekeeping genes scCDC. FastCAR targets differential expression; in asthma biopsies 214 genes were differentially expressed only after correction FastCAR. Uncorrected ambient genes appeared among DEGs and enriched pathways in PBMC and fetal liver data arora-2025, and ambient RNA defined some previously annotated neuronal types in brain nuclei data caglayan-2022.

Damage or biology: how to tell

Mito fraction alone is a poor damage marker. In sorted cells, dying (annexin V positive) cells had a median mito fraction of 3.13%, no higher than live cells (3.4%); only dead cells were high (29.9%) oflanagan-2019. A mito cut-off therefore removes dead cells, not early apoptotic ones, and also removes healthy cells with a high baseline. Baselines vary by tissue osorio-cai-2021 and by cell line: median mito fraction across CCLE lines ran from 4% in glioblastoma to 14% in head and neck cancer, and higher mito fraction was associated with higher IC50, that is, drug resistance mito-filter-resistant-cells. Filtering on mito in a drug screen can therefore remove the resistant cells selectively.

Signals that separate them:

  • Nuclear fraction. A damaged cell has lost cytoplasm, so its remaining reads are nuclear (unspliced). DropletQC's damaged calls rose with apoptosis in staurosporine-treated HEK293 cells and had higher mito DropletQC. Requires BAM or spliced/unspliced counts.
  • Joint metrics. Compromised cells combine high mito with few genes detected; healthy high-mito cells keep normal complexity miQC. MALAT1 and intronic fraction add nuclear-retention evidence scQCenrich; MitoChontrol's removed cells were enriched for MALAT1 in 7 of 9 pancreatic tumour samples with significant differences MitoChontrol.
  • Within-type comparison. Thresholds computed within a cell type, cluster or sample avoid removing a whole type for its baseline ddqc, pipeComp.
  • Ambient-like profile. Droplets whose profile resembles the soup are empty or lysed, whatever their UMI count EmptyDrops.

Stress is not damage. Enzymatic dissociation at 37 C induces immediate-early and heat-shock genes in subsets of cells van-den-brink-2017; a 512-gene core set (FOS, FOSB, ATF3, heat-shock genes) was conserved across tumours and lines and largely avoided by cold protease at 6 C oflanagan-2019. These cells are intact; score and model the signature rather than filtering them. Preparation choices also change who survives: cold dissociation of mouse kidney recovered 330 podocytes (2.78%) against 3 (0.03%) warm; cryopreserved suspensions gave ~30% fewer high-quality cells than fresh or methanol-fixed ones; single nuclei gave more genes per barcode (median 1,819 vs 981) but fewer immune cells (0.73% vs 6.03%) denisenko-2020. In tumours, cells and nuclei recovered the same types in different proportions (PMID 32405060). Fixation designs for pooled screens are covered in the design review (Methanol fixation, 10x Chromium Flex).

Hypotheses and open questions

  • condition-aware-qc-audit: drugs move the very metrics QC uses (global transcription, PMID 34159316; mito fraction, mito-filter-resistant-cells). A global fixed threshold then removes cells at a rate the drug sets, while thresholds computed per condition hide a toxic drug's damage. Thresholds per cell type and batch, plus a table of losses per condition and QC step, would expose the bias. No study has measured it.
  • Open: no benchmark tests adaptive QC or cell calling on drug-treated cells. In a pooled lane the ambient profile mixes every condition, so a toxic drug's lysed cells contaminate all others in that lane; whether per-lane correction removes false drug-response genes in pseudobulk has not been tested. Nie et al.'s abstract and results disagree on which tool estimates contamination best.

Recommendations for low-cell multiplexed drug screens

Ranked by expected gain per unit of effort. Gains are from the cited settings, not from drug screens, which have no direct benchmark.

  1. Audit losses per condition before choosing thresholds. Tabulate cells removed by cell calling, each QC metric and doublet calling, for every drug and dose. Set thresholds per cell type and lane (or plate), never per drug. Gain: makes condition-dependent loss visible; no measured number. Data: filtered matrix, tag assignments. condition-aware-qc-audit
  2. Replace fixed mito and gene cut-offs with lenient adaptive ones. Use 5 MADs within cell type and lane MAD-based adaptive QC thresholds, or a mixture model (miQC, MitoChontrol) where mito is high at baseline, as in many cancer lines. Gain: 41% vs 19% removed miQC; 69.4% vs 95.4% retained ddqc. Data: filtered matrix.
  3. Re-call cells from the raw matrix. Run emptyDrops (lower bound 100) on the raw matrix rather than trusting the 500-UMI candidate floor of Cell Ranger-style calling; consider CB2; check rescued barcodes with nuclear fraction and tag strength. Gain: 4-81% more cells in tissue data, self-reported CB2. Data: raw matrix; tag counts help Tag-guided rescue of low-RNA cells.
  4. Use nuclear fraction, not mito alone, to call damage. Run DropletQC or scQCenrich; remove cells flagged damaged by both nuclear fraction and low complexity; keep high-mito cells with normal complexity. Report damaged share per condition. Gain: keeps intact high-mito cells; flags damage that mito misses in early apoptosis. Data: BAM or spliced/unspliced counts.
  5. Correct ambient RNA per lane before differential expression. CellBender remove-background with a raw matrix and GPU, DecontX with a filtered matrix only, SoupX reduced mode as the conservative option when contamination is low. Check that control-only genes do not appear in treated cells after correction. Gain: Slc34a1 leakage 60% to 7% (CellBender) janssen-2023; risk of over-correction on clean samples cargnelli-2026. Data: raw matrix (CellBender, SoupX full mode).
  6. Do not drop cells on RNA doublet scores or high-UMI caps alone. Use tags for cross-sample doublets (demultiplexing review); run scDblFinder per lane only where cell types are mixed. Gain: avoids losing large healthy cells pipeComp; in single-line screens RNA detectors reach mean AUPRC of only 0.13-0.34 singletcode-2024. Data: filtered matrix, tag counts.
  7. At the bench: remove dead and apoptotic cells before loading (PMID 31603610), use cold dissociation for tissue oflanagan-2019, and prefer fixation or nuclei when samples must wait denisenko-2020.

Chapter 03

Statistics with few cells: more signal per cell and per condition

29 records reviewed here, 35 records cited in the text

In this chapter

  1. The short answer
  2. Standard practice
  3. Benchmarked state of the art
  4. Published but not independently benchmarked
  5. What the evidence says about deep models and imputation
  6. One culture per condition: what the p-value means
  7. Hypotheses and open questions
  8. Ranked recommendations for low-cell multiplexed drug screens
  9. Records in this chapter

Scope: what to do statistically when a condition has few cells, few replicates, or only one culture, with high-multiplex drug screens as the lead case. Literature checked to October 2026. Every PMID and DOI below was resolved against PubMed, Crossref or DataCite.

The short answer

Most of the extra signal available from a low-cell condition comes from borrowing information, not from squeezing individual cells harder. Borrowing works across genes (empirical Bayes variance moderation), across the conditions of a screen (one shared model, doses as a trend, multivariate shrinkage), and across the genes of a program (footprint scores). None of it creates replication. The unit of inference has to stay the independent culture, well or donor, and in benchmarks the methods that respect that unit are both the best calibrated and the most concordant with bulk RNA-seq. Three findings carry most of the weight:

  • Across 18 datasets with matched bulk RNA-seq, all six top-ranked of 14 DE methods were pseudobulk methods, and cell-level methods called hundreds of DE genes between randomly assigned replicates with no perturbation (Squair 2021, PMID 34584091) squair-2021.
  • Splitting cells into random groups and calling them replicates brought the bias and the false discoveries back: pseudo-replicates shrank variance most for highly expressed genes across 46 datasets (Squair 2021, PMID 34584091). This is the split-well design many drug screens use.
  • Deep perturbation models have not yet beaten additive or linear baselines in independent benchmarks (Ahlmann-Eltze 2025, PMID 40759747), and imputation mostly erases small effects (Hou 2020, PMID 32854757), so neither is a substitute for replicate-level statistics in a screen whose effects are often small.

Standard practice

Pseudobulk. Counts are summed per replicate sample and cell type, then tested with bulk tools (edgeR, DESeq2, limma-voom) Pseudobulk differential expression. The cross-modality best-practice review states that pseudobulk methods with sum aggregation, and mixed models such as MAST with a random effect, were superior to naive cell-level tests such as the Wilcoxon test (Heumos 2023, heumos-2023). Earlier work reached the same conclusion with aggregateBioVar: naive tests inflate the FDR when expression varies between subjects (Thurman 2021, PMID 33970215).

muscat packages pseudobulk and mixed-model tests plus a simulator that later benchmarks reuse (Crowell 2020, PMID 33257685) muscat. Its pbDS default excludes any cluster-sample with fewer than 10 cells.

Empirical Bayes moderation is the oldest and most reliable way to gain power with 2 to 3 replicates. limma shrinks each gene's variance toward a trend fitted across all genes (Smyth 2004, PMID 16646809; Ritchie 2015, PMID 25605792); edgeR does the same for dispersions, and edgeR v4 revised its quasi-likelihood method to improve accuracy for small counts (Chen 2025, PMID 39844453); apeglm shrinks noisy fold changes (Zhu 2019, PMID 30395178) Empirical Bayes moderation. It borrows across genes, not across conditions, and it cannot moderate a variance that was never estimated: one culture per condition leaves zero residual degrees of freedom for that condition.

Sample weights instead of removal. limma's voomWithQualityWeights estimates a variance factor per sample and down-weights noisy samples rather than discarding them, which its authors report gives more power and fewer false discoveries than either removing or equally weighting such samples (Liu 2015, PMID 25925576) voomWithQualityWeights.

Minimum-cells rules. Floors such as muscat's 10 cells or dreamlet's 5 cells per sample (with at least 4 samples per cluster) are software defaults Minimum-cells rules for pseudobulk samples. The only direct evidence found is a matched scRNA-seq and bulk comparison of the same purified cells: about 2,000 cells per cluster recovered most DEGs with modest bulk differences, while 50 to 100 cells recovered most DEGs with extremely small bulk p-values or abundance above a few hundred TPM (Liu 2023, PMID 37394518). That study compares cell populations from one aliquot, so it says how many cells are needed to see strong effects, not how many replicates are needed to trust them.

Responder identification in CRISPR screens. Mixscape subtracts each targeted cell's 20 nearest control neighbours to form a perturbation signature, then classifies cells as perturbed or escaping; in its ECCITE-seq screen 115 of 278 IFNGR2-targeted cells escaped (Papalexi 2021, PMID 33649593) Mixscape. The best-practice review lists it for perturbation screens (Heumos 2023, heumos-2023). Drug responses are graded rather than binary; the perturbation-response score models partial responses (Song 2025, PMID 40011559).

Benchmarked state of the art

Pseudobulk is the benchmark leader. In an independent comparison of 18 methods, pseudobulk methods had the highest average AUROC and clearly the best F1; naive cell-level methods had the highest sensitivity but many false positives, and modelling subjects as latent variables did not fix them (Junttila 2022, PMID 35880426) junttila-2022. Sum aggregation generally beat mean, and sensitivity rose with the number of subjects for every method. A 2025 benchmark of DESeq2, MAST, DREAM, scVI, permutation, distinct, the t-test and hierarchical bootstrapping found no single-cell-specific method better than pseudobulk DESeq2 on individual datasets, and recommended DREAM as a quality and runtime compromise at atlas scale (Hafner 2025, PMID 40794957). For data with batches, modelling batch as a covariate beat analysing batch-corrected data across 46 workflows (Nguyen 2023, PMID 36944632).

Mixed models: close, contested. Zimmerman and colleagues found pseudobulk conservative and underpowered relative to generalized linear mixed models with a random effect per individual (Zimmerman 2021, PMID 33531494). Re-running their simulation with the Matthews correlation coefficient, Murphy and Skene found pseudobulk mean had sensitivity above 0.9 at equal type 1 error while every other method was below 0.9, across 5 to 40 individuals and 50 to 500 cells (Murphy 2022, PMID 36550119), though they attribute the mean-over-sum advantage to a missing normalisation step in the simulator. The reply argues that MCC can reward tests whose type 1 error exceeds 0.50 (Zimmerman 2022, PMID 36550147) pseudobulk-vs-mixed-debate. Lee 2024 narrowed the gap analytically: count pseudobulk with the right offset has the same point estimates and standard errors as a GLMM and runs more than 10 times faster (Lee 2024, PMID 39115884).

NEBULA is the one mixed-model tool that topped an independent benchmark: NEBULA-HL and glmmTMB outperformed 10 other methods, pseudobulk included, in a 12-method simulation of multi-subject 10x data (Gagnon 2022, PMID 35743881) NEBULA. Its own authors note that tests of a subject-level variable were highly sensitive to the subject variance estimate when subjects were few (He 2021, PMID 34040149), which is exactly the low-replicate case.

Published but not independently benchmarked

dreamlet: keep small samples, weight them. dreamlet fits precision-weighted linear mixed models to pseudobulk, initialising weights from a Poisson model in which more cells and reads per sample mean higher precision, then applies empirical Bayes moderation (Hoffman 2026, PMID 42778542) dreamlet. Its authors report that the Poisson weights improved performance over the unweighted model, that it controlled the permuted-label false positive rate (target 5%) where the muscat limma-voom path and GLMMs were inflated, and that it pseudobulked 2.2 million cells in 10 minutes with 20 GB (preprint, PMID 36993704). Plates, pools and processing batches can enter as random effects.

Unequal group variances. voomByGroup fits a mean-variance trend per group and voomQWB one weight per group; their authors show both improve error control and power when pseudobulk groups have unequal variances, which they found common (You 2023, PMID 37147723) voomByGroup and voomQWB. Both need several replicates per group.

Pseudosamples for removing plate effects, not for testing. RUVIII-PBPS resamples cells within biology-by-batch groups to build artificial pseudobulks used only to estimate unwanted-variation factors; it works with one single-cell sample per group, reduced processing-cohort silhouette from 0.17 to 0.06 in a real dataset, and controlled FDR where standard RUV could not be used (Prieto León 2025, PMID 41368194) RUVIII with pseudobulk pseudosamples. It is the legitimate use of resampled cells: the DE test still runs on real replicates.

Borrowing across conditions. mashr learns covariance patterns of effects across conditions and shrinks each condition's estimate toward them. On GTEx eQTLs in 44 tissues it called 47% of effects significant at local false sign rate below 0.05, against 13% for condition-by-condition analysis (Urbut 2019, PMID 30478440) mashr. A drug screen has the same shape (many drugs, shared pathways), and contrasts against one shared vehicle control are handled through a reference condition in the package. No single-cell drug-screen benchmark was found.

Doses as a trend. sci-Plex modelled each gene as a function of dose by generalized linear regression and found 6,238 genes with dose-dependent expression in at least one of three cell lines (FDR below 5%) at a median of only 100 to 200 cells per condition (Srivatsan 2020, PMID 31806696) sci-Plex Dose-response modelling across doses. General-purpose curve fitting is available in drc (Ritz 2015, PMID 26717316) and for omics in DRomics (Larras 2018, PMID 30444611). Small effects agreed less well with bulk in sci-Plex.

Effect-size summaries for whole perturbations. TRADE models the distribution of true DE effects from pseudobulk estimates and their standard errors. In five Perturb-seq screens, FDR-significant genes explained only 13% to 36% of each perturbation's estimated transcriptome-wide impact; a typical perturbation affected about 45 genes (Nadig 2025, PMID 40259084) TRADE. scDist answers "did anything change" with a mixed model on distances between condition means (Nicol 2024, PMID 39218971) scDist. The E-test of scPerturb is a permutation test over cells (Peidli 2024, PMID 38279009); with one well per condition it tests whether two wells differ.

Factor models across perturbations. GSFA infers gene modules and each perturbation's effect on them; in its authors' simulations its calls kept false discovery proportions well below 0.05 while edgeR and t-test calls were inflated, with more power than t-test, edgeR-QLF and MAST (Zhou 2023, PMID 37770710) GSFA.

Program-level tests. decoupler scores pathway and transcription-factor activity from footprint gene sets (PROGENy, DoRothEA, CollecTRI); simple linear models and a consensus score best predicted perturbed regulators (Badia-i-Mompel 2022, PMID 36699385) decoupler / decoupleR. Footprints derived from bulk worked on scRNA-seq and partly beat AUCell/SCENIC and metaVIPER, though PROGENy's AUROC fell from 0.724 to 0.636 as gene coverage dropped (Holland 2020, PMID 32051003, same group). Scorer choice matters: Pagoda2 led 7 tools on 32 datasets (Zhang 2020, PMID 33209207); bulk-style scorers are biased by genes detected per cell (Noureen 2022, PMID 35212622); and in a pseudobulk preprint benchmark, rank-based AUCell and UCell inverted the sign of a pathway in 40% of simulated replicates under high competitor burden (Alakwaa 2026, PMID 42466400, preprint) signature-scoring-evidence.

What the evidence says about deep models and imputation

Prediction models. Five foundation models plus GEARS and CPA were compared with deliberately simple baselines; on 62 held-out double perturbations every model had prediction error substantially higher than an additive baseline, and none beat a "no change" baseline at finding interactions (Ahlmann-Eltze 2025, PMID 40759747) ahlmann-eltze-2025. Two further studies found simple baselines ahead of deep models, a training-mean baseline beating scGPT and scFoundation among them (Csendes 2025, PMID 40269681; Wong 2025, PMID 40407144). The finding is disputed: with calibrated metrics and a positive-control baseline, deep models beat uninformative baselines across 14 datasets (Miller 2026, PMID 42823510). A 13-method, 25-dataset comparison including two drug-response sets found models conservative, with fine-tuned foundation models compressing variance and underestimating synergy, and no method generalising across cell types (Li 2026, PMID 42715312).

CPA and chemCPA decompose cells into a basal state plus perturbation and covariate embeddings with learned dose-response curves, and predict unseen doses and combinations (Lotfollahi 2023, PMID 37154091; chemCPA, Hetzel 2022, doi 10.48550/arXiv.2204.13545) CPA and chemCPA. The CPA paper itself assumes enough cells per condition to fit the latent space, the opposite of the low-cell case. scGen, the earlier model from the same group, used latent vector arithmetic (Lotfollahi 2019, PMID 31363220). MrVI adds a sample-aware latent space; on sci-Plex its drug-dose distances agreed better with Connectivity Map than PCA- or scVI-based groupings (Boyeau 2025, PMID 41083897) MrVI. With one well per drug-dose, its "sample" is the well, so drug and well cannot be separated. scVI's Bayesian DE (Boyeau 2023, PMID 37192164) scVI differential expression was no better than pseudobulk DESeq2 in the nested benchmark (Hafner 2025, PMID 40794957).

Imputation. Smoothing methods (MAGIC, knn-smooth, DCA) created many false-positive DE genes and correlations; SAVER was least likely to, and the authors recommend testing on un-imputed data (Andrews 2018, PMID 30906525) imputation-de-evidence. In an 18-method evaluation, 13 of 16 methods raised overlap with bulk DEGs when effects were large, but only 2 of 16 did when effects were small (Hou 2020, PMID 32854757). Drug screens at low cell numbers are mostly in the small-effect regime.

One culture per condition: what the p-value means

Sample size in a cell experiment is the number of independent applications of the treatment, not the number of cells measured (Lazic 2018, PMID 29617358; Vaux 2012, PMID 22421999; Blainey 2014, PMID 25317452) cell-subsample-pseudoreplicates. In a survey of animal studies only 22% replicated the right unit and 46% pseudoreplicated (Lazic 2018, PMID 29617358). When one well's cells are split into subsets, any test compares the two wells: a small p-value says the wells differ by more than cell sampling would explain, and any difference between the two cultures, not only the drug, can produce that. Squair 2021 showed this directly (PMID 34584091). Effect sizes, rankings and dose trends from such data remain useful, as long as they are reported as single-culture estimates.

Hypotheses and open questions

Pooled variance for unreplicated drugs (hypothesis). In one linear model over all wells, drugs with a single well can be tested against a residual variance estimated from replicated wells, such as many vehicle wells pooled-variance-unreplicated-drugs. The assumption that unreplicated drugs share that variance is the one voomByGroup found often fails (You 2023, PMID 37147723). Untested in single-cell screens.

A well-to-well null (hypothesis). Compute the same statistic for vehicle-vs-vehicle well pairs and use its distribution as the threshold for drug-vs-vehicle calls control-well-null, generalising the mock comparisons of Squair 2021 (PMID 34584091) and Junttila 2022 (PMID 35880426). It needs vehicle wells spread over plates and positions.

Open questions: whether cell-count precision weights (dreamlet) or quality weights beat minimum-cells cut-offs in screens with 1 to 3 wells per drug; whether mashr or dose models improve calibrated recall on a screen with held-out replicate wells; and whether any perturbation model beats an additive baseline for unseen drugs at 50 to 200 cells per condition.

Power. hierarchicell simulates within-sample correlation and shows that calculators counting cells instead of independent units grossly overestimate power (Zimmerman 2021, PMID 33932993) hierarchicell; scPower models cost against samples, cells and depth and finds shallow sequencing of many cells more powerful than deep sequencing of few (Schmid 2021, PMID 34785648) scPower; powsimR is an older simulation framework (Vieth 2017, PMID 29036287). Design-side trade-offs (wells, plates, multiplexing) are covered in the screen design chapter, for example sci-Plex and Tahoe-100M.

Chapter 04

Designing the next screen: more usable cells and true replicates per condition

26 records reviewed here, 28 records cited in the text

In this chapter

  1. The short answer
  2. What the large screens did
  3. Platform and reagent comparisons
  4. Sample tags
  5. Loading and doublets
  6. Combinatorial indexing and collisions
  7. Commercial kits
  8. Fixation and storage
  9. Trade-offs: cells, conditions, depth and replicates
  10. Hypotheses and open questions
  11. Ranked recommendations for the next high-multiplex drug screen
  12. Sources
  13. Records in this chapter

Scope: experimental design for high-multiplex drug (pharmacotranscriptomic) single-cell screens, where many conditions each get few cells. This page covers what the large screens did, how the platforms and sample tags compare on cell recovery, and which trade-offs matter. Calling tools for hashtags and genotypes are covered in the demultiplexing review; statistics for few cells are in the low-cell statistics review.

The short answer

Four design choices change usable cells and true replicates per condition the most.

  1. Replicate the treatment, not the cell. Cells from one well are pseudoreplicates; treating them as independent inflates type 1 error (Zimmerman 2021; see squair-2021). sci-Plex treated every compound-dose in duplicate wells with positions randomised between plates, and the duplicates agreed at pseudobulk r = 0.99 (Srivatsan 2020, sci-Plex). sci-Plex-GxE repeated each condition in two independent transductions (sci-Plex-GxE). Tahoe-100M, the largest screen, ran one well per drug-dose, so its median of 1,287 cells per condition comes from a single well (Tahoe-100M). See Independent replicate wells or cultures per condition.
  2. Tag every sample, then load more cells per lane. With hashtags or genotypes, cross-sample doublets can be removed, so lanes can be overloaded. Cell Hashing modelled about 4x more singlets at a matched unresolved multiplet rate (Stoeckius 2018, Cell Hashing), and an independent cost model found overloading raised power under a fixed budget (Schmid 2021, scPower). The cost is non-linear: capturing 48% more cells raised doublets by 125% and unassigned barcodes by 325% (Mylka 2022, mylka-2022-hashing-comparison). See Superloading with sample multiplexing.
  3. Fix at harvest. Fixed cells stop changing while plates wait. After 4 weeks at -80 C, fixed (10x Flex) and cryopreserved (HIVE) leukocytes kept fragile granulocytes better than fresh 10x 3' processing across nine sites (ABRF 2026, abrf-preservation-2026). Fixation is also what makes plate-native multiplexing possible (SPLiT-seq / Parse Evercode, sci-Plex, 10x Chromium Flex).
  4. Measure where cells are lost. Losses between input and final data are large and differ by platform: about 53% of input PBMCs were recovered with 10x against 27% with Parse (Xie 2024), and 42.7% against 16.5% in organoids (Sarieva 2026) (split-pool-input-recovery). Nucleus hashing left about 33% of nuclei after its extra washes (Gaublomme 2019, Nucleus hashing). In Tahoe-100M, 95.6 million of 153 million barcoded cells (about 62%) passed full filters.

How many cells per condition is enough depends on the question. scPerturb, re-analysing 44 public perturbation datasets, recommends at least 200-500 cells per perturbation and about 1,000 UMIs per cell to tell a perturbation from control (Peidli 2024, scperturb). MIX-Seq's downsampling found that tens of cells per condition were enough to estimate each cell line's mean response (McFarland 2020, MIX-Seq).

Sources: Srivatsan 2020; McFaline-Figueroa 2024; McFarland 2020; Tahoe-100M Cell abstract (2026) and bioRxiv preprint methods (2025). sci-Plex vehicle wells: 96, calculated as 4,608 drug and vehicle wells minus 4,512 drug wells.

What these show:

  • Pooling lines multiplies conditions per well. Tahoe-100M gets one condition per line in every well, about 50 per well. The price is coupling: every line in a well shares that well's handling, so the lines are contexts, not replicates of the treatment, and resistant or fast-growing lines take over after cytotoxic drugs. MIX-Seq detected 97 of 99 lines with at least 20 cells per condition, and Tahoe-100M dropped 3 of 50 lines for consistently low counts and excluded conditions under 50 cells (Cell villages).
  • Cell number per well is itself a readout. sci-Plex estimated viability from hash-based nucleus counts per dose; MIX-Seq measured drug-induced shifts in each line's share of the pool. Pooling equal cell numbers per well before barcoding, as Tahoe-100M did, equalises conditions but removes that readout unless cells are counted first (count-then-balance-input).
  • Controls were placed differently. Tahoe-100M kept control-media wells at fixed positions H11 and H12 of each plate and compared drugs with DMSO controls from the same plate; the preprint does not state how many DMSO wells each plate held. sci-Plex randomised positions between replicate plates. Neither reported a test of well-position effects.

Platform and reagent comparisons

Sample tags

Mylka 2022 compared tags against genotype ground truth on four cell lines, their nuclei, PBMCs and mouse tissues (mylka-2022-hashing-comparison):

InputAntibody (TotalSeq)Lipid / cholesterol oligosMeasure
Cell lines1.1% (A), 1.8% (C)7% (MULTI-seq LMO), 21% (custom LMO)barcodes left unassigned
Cell linesabout 0.1%0.89% (MULTI-seq), 2.68% (custom)tag swaps among singlets
NucleiOCA 0.51-0.54 (0.65 after tuning)OCA 0.84 (cholesterol)agreement with genotype
PBMCsOCA 0.96 (TotalSeq-B)OCA 0.93 (10x CellPlex)agreement with genotype

Antibodies worked best on whole cells; lipid-based tags worked best on nuclei (cholesterol oligos) and on mouse brain cells; antibodies did better on spleen and lung. Tags can also rescue cells: in a tumour sample, 90.8% of sequenced neutrophils fell below the Cell Ranger UMI threshold and were kept by MULTI-seq classification (McGinnis 2019, MULTI-seq). sci-Plex labels nuclei with unmodified polyadenylated oligos during lysis in the well; in a human-mouse test it recovered a median of 270 hash UMIs per cell with 99.1% agreement with species, and the label survived a freeze-thaw cycle (Srivatsan 2020).

Loading and doublets

10x guidance quoted by Mylka 2022 puts the multiplet rate near 0.8% per 1,000 captured cells (vendor-reported). Only multiplets that join different samples are visible to tags, about 1 - 1/N of them for N equal samples (87.5% for eight samples in Gaublomme 2019). Cell Hashing superloaded an 8-donor pool and observed 14,002 singlets with 2,974 identifiable multiplets (Stoeckius 2018). Nucleus hashing loaded 500 to 4,500 nuclei per ul with comparable cell types and genes per nucleus (Gaublomme 2019). MIX-Seq loaded up to 40,000 cells per 10x channel. scPower notes that observed doublet rates ran above its model, so modelled gains from overloading are best treated as upper bounds (Schmid 2021).

Combinatorial indexing and collisions

In split-pool and combinatorial designs the doublet equivalent is a barcode collision, set by cells per final well relative to the number of barcode combinations.

  • SPLiT-seq: 0.1% mouse-human collisions in a 1,758-cell mixing test, and 2.5% expected for 150,000 nuclei with 48 x 96 x 96 x 14 combinations (Rosenberg 2018, SPLiT-seq / Parse Evercode).
  • sci-Plex: varying nuclei per PCR well produced collision rates of 7-23%, matching prediction; well hashes flagged 95.5% of interspecies collisions and also exposed within-species ones (Srivatsan 2020).
  • scifi-RNA-seq: preindexing in cells plus overloaded droplets gave up to 150,000 cells per 10x channel, with recovered cells rising linearly from 15,300 to 765,000 loaded nuclei; preindexing itself kept only 53.3% (cell lines) and 41.1% (primary) of nuclei (Datlinger 2021, scifi-RNA-seq).
  • UDA-seq: droplet barcodes first, then plate post-indexing; 1.23% collisions against 6.29% expected from droplets alone, with cell recovery of about 57% for 3' RNA (Li 2025, UDA-seq).
  • sci-RNA-seq3: about 2 million nuclei from 61 embryos in one experiment; the optimised protocol costs about 1 cent per cell in reagents and uses DSP/methanol fixation, which gave more UMIs than paraformaldehyde (Cao 2019; Martin 2023; sci-RNA-seq3).
  • Tahoe-100M split its barcoded cells into 1,786 sublibraries of about 100,000 cells each.

Commercial kits

De Simone 2025 ran nine kits on PBMCs from one donor (de-simone-2025). 10x Flex (fixed RNA profiling) ranked best overall and in the top tier for genes per cell; Flex, 10x 3' and BD gave the most UMIs per cell. Cells recovered against the targeted number ranged from about 70% (BD) to 122% (Parse); Parse and Scale were run once each because of kit cost. Recovery against target is not recovery against input: on PBMCs Parse recovered about 27% of input cells against 53% for 10x, and about 85% of Parse reads carried a valid barcode against 98% for 10x (Xie 2024). On cerebellar organoids, recovery was 16.5% for Parse against 42.7% for 10x, but more Parse cells passed QC (95.6% against 87.2%) and fewer showed a stress signature; the authors suggest the stress arises while 10x cells wait unfixed and pass through the microfluidics (Sarieva 2026). On mouse thymocytes Parse detected about twice as many genes as 10x, while 10x had lower technical variability (Filippov 2024).

For Flex specifically: its probes do not cover most mitochondrial transcripts, so the usual mitochondrial-fraction filter loses meaning (ABRF 2026). Core-facility guidance relaying the 10x protocol recommends at least 25,000 cells per fixation (10x support advises 75,000) and warns that targeting more than about 13,000 cells per sample pushes multiplets above 5% (EPFL GECF guidelines, 2025). 10x announced in October 2025 a plate-format Flex for up to 384 samples and 100 million cells per week (vendor-reported, not independently tested).

Fixation and storage

  • Methanol: no change in genes or UMIs per cell after storage for weeks (Alles 2017). On hiPSC-derived neural cells it kept composition closest to fresh, while DMSO cryopreservation gave the most complex libraries but shifted composition and induced stress and apoptosis genes (Gutierrez-Franco 2023). Wohnhaas 2019 preferred DMSO cryopreservation in other cell types, so the choice is cell-type dependent (Methanol fixation).
  • DSP (reversible crosslinker): fresh against fixed K562 bulk r above 0.93, fixed replicates stored 3 or 7 days r about 0.97; slightly lower cDNA yield and some 3' bias; fixed cells keep propidium iodide, so viability at fixation can be recorded (Attar 2018, DSP reversible fixation).
  • FixNCut: DSP fixation of tissue before dissociation preserved composition and reduced stress signatures (Jimenez-Gracia 2024, FixNCut).

Trade-offs: cells, conditions, depth and replicates

Depth against cells. Under a fixed budget, shallow sequencing of more cells gave higher power than deep sequencing of fewer cells across platforms (Schmid 2021), and lower coverage of more individuals raised cell-type eQTL power (Mandric 2020). For estimating gene distributions, the optimum was about one read per cell per gene (Zhang 2020, sequencing-depth-allocation). In scPerturb, the number of significant perturbations stopped rising near 500 UMIs per cell. Tahoe-100M cells had a median of 1,890 transcripts. Taken together, these results suggest that depth well beyond about 1,000 UMIs per cell buys less than more cells or more wells for condition-level questions.

Cells against conditions. The number of significant perturbations fell as scPerturb subsampled cells per perturbation, and only some datasets reached saturation at their full cell count. sci-Plex, at a median of 100-200 cells per condition, had 107 of 188 drugs significant by E-test. sci-Plex-GxE ran about 35 cells per gene-by-drug condition and pooled guides per gene to compensate.

Conditions against replicates. Tahoe-100M put its budget into conditions; sci-Plex and sci-Plex-GxE paid for a second independent well or transduction. Without a second well, the drug effect cannot be separated from that well's handling. Pseudobulk testing needs the well as its unit (Zimmerman 2021; squair-2021).

Lines against replicates. Pooled lines raise conditions per well and share one environment, which removes line-by-well confounding (Wells 2023, Cell villages), but they do not replicate the treatment.

Doses and time points. Dose series let information be shared across conditions (sci-Plex fitted dose-response models to estimate the transcriptional potency of HDAC inhibitors). MIX-Seq found DMSO cells did not differ across five time points and pooled them, which raised control cells per comparison.

Hypotheses and open questions

  • Scattered vehicle controls. In bulk drug-testing plates, normalisation broke down above about 20% hits per plate when controls sat at the plate edge, while scattered controls with Loess reduced row, column and edge effects (Mpindi 2015, simulated 384-well plates). No single-cell study found here measured well-position effects (scattered-vehicle-controls).
  • How many DMSO wells? sci-Plex used 96 vehicle wells for 4,512 drug wells (calculated from reported totals); the Tahoe-100M preprint does not state its DMSO well count. No study justified its number.
  • Count, then balance. Counting cells per well before pooling equal numbers would keep viability as a readout and equalise cells per condition (count-then-balance-input). Untested.
  • Cytotoxic dropout. Cells are fewest where drug effects are largest. Seeding more cells in high-dose wells, or pooling replicate wells for those doses, has not been evaluated.
  • Nuclei or whole cells for drug response. sci-Plex works on nuclei; MIX-Seq and Tahoe-100M on whole cells. No head-to-head comparison of drug-response signal between nuclei and cells was found.
  • Flex in small wells. Fixation inputs of 25,000-75,000 cells per sample may exceed what a treated 96-well well yields; whether plate-format Flex removes that limit has not been independently reported.

Ranked recommendations for the next high-multiplex drug screen

  1. Two or more independently treated wells per condition, with drug and dose positions randomised between replicate plates (sci-Plex). Pay for it with depth, not with replication.
  2. Tag every well at harvest and fix. Cholesterol oligos for nuclei, antibodies for whole cells (Mylka 2022), or polyA hash oligos when the readout is sci-RNA-seq (sci-Plex). Use the tags for doublet removal and for counting cells per well.
  3. Target about 200-500 cells per condition and about 1,000 UMIs per cell when the question is whether a drug changes the cell distribution (scPerturb); tens of cells can do for mean-shift profiles (MIX-Seq).
  4. Overload with tags, after a pilot loading series that measures doublets and unassigned barcodes, since both rise faster than cells captured (Mylka 2022).
  5. Pool cell lines only as extra contexts, balanced at seeding and with genotype references, and never count them as replicates.
  6. Log losses at each step: cells seeded, cells at harvest, cells into barcoding, barcodes passing QC; report recovery against input.
  7. Put vehicle wells on every plate, scattered across rows, columns and edges (hypothesis, from bulk screening).
  8. Pick the platform by input and plex: Flex for sensitivity and fragile cells when per-sample input is large; split-pool kits or sci-RNA-seq3 for 96-384 plate-native samples, accepting lower input recovery.
